articles.title: What happened to Kick streamer Gtwist? Livestream clip sparks debate after alleged confrontation with his father
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Young Kick streamer Gtwist has become the center of a major online discussion after a disturbing clip from his livestream spread across X on August 30.
articles.body: Young Kick streamer Gtwist has become the center of a major online discussion after a disturbing clip from his livestream spread across X on August 30, 2026. The footage appears to show an adult man, identified in reports as Gtwist’s father, entering his room and grabbing him during the broadcast. Gtwist appears upset and later ends the stream. The clip has since been widely shared, but important details remain unclear. His exact age has not been independently confirmed, and there is also no clear public evidence showing whether the incident was real or staged.Gtwist appears to break down during livestreamThere is limited verified information about Gtwist outside his streaming activity. Current reports describe him as a young Kick streamer and minor, while some posts online claim he is around 13. That age has not been independently confirmed.The clip that went viral is around two minutes long. Gtwist can be seen sitting at his gaming setup when an adult man enters the room. Reports identify the man as his father. He appears to make comments about Gtwist’s voice before grabbing him around the neck area and pulling him backward.Gtwist then appears visibly distressed and begins crying before the stream ends.A post sharing the footage claimed it was recorded shortly before the VOD was deleted. The clip spread rapidly on X, with copies appearing on different accounts after the original stream was no longer available. One video tracker showed the clip had reached millions of views within hours.The footage has led to concern about Gtwist’s safety, especially because reports describe him as a minor. However, viewers do not have enough verified information to establish everything that happened before or after the portion shown online.Gtwist Kick ban adds to questions around the incidentGtwist’s Kick account was reportedly banned shortly after the incident. Al Bawaba reported that Kick was investigating the footage because it appeared to involve violence and a minor.The reported ban has become another part of the discussion, although a platform ban by itself does not confirm what happened inside Gtwist’s home or establish that authorities took action.Some reports also said Gtwist later indicated that he was fine and planned to stream again. Those claims have not been independently verified.The biggest question now is whether the incident shown in the clip was genuine. Many viewers reacted with concern after seeing Gtwist appear to cry, while others questioned whether the confrontation could have been staged for attention.One X user wrote:“If it’s real the dad is a huge loser. If it’s scripted the dad is a huge loser.”Another commenter said:“We need a license to parent man because I’m tired of these low life’s becoming dads.”Others were more skeptical. One user wrote:“you’re dumb as fk if you think this is real.”That disagreement has made it difficult to separate confirmed details from speculation. At present, the widely shared footage is the main evidence available to the public, while claims about Gtwist’s exact age, his family and what happened away from the camera remain unverified.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: New Mexico man accused of fatally shooting cousin after argument over enchiladas
articles.summary: Police say the men had been drinking and arguing before a fistfight broke out. A witness said the victim was walking away when Ervin Gutierrez pulled a gun and opened fire.
articles.body: A New Mexico man is accused of fatally shooting his cousin after an evening of drinking escalated from an argument over enchiladas into a fistfight, according to an arrest warrant. Ervin Joaquin Gutierrez, 22, is charged with an open count of murder in the Aug. 27 killing of Nathaniel Cavazos at an apartment complex in Albuquerque. Gutierrez was arrested by Albuquerque police Friday evening and booked into the Metropolitan Detention Center shortly after midnight Saturday, according to jail records. He is being held on an open count of murder. Albuquerque police responded to a shooting shortly before 11 p.m. and found Cavazos unresponsive in a pool of blood on the walkway between apartment buildings. He had been shot at least once and died from his injuries, according to the warrant affidavit. A cousin of both men who told police he witnessed the shooting said Gutierrez had arrived earlier that afternoon to visit. The three later bought groceries, returned to the apartment and cooked green enchiladas while drinking alcohol, according to the affidavit. The witness told authorities tension began when Gutierrez repeatedly claimed the chile on his enchiladas was hotter than the chile on Cavazos’ plate and challenged him to eat some. Cavazos responded that they had all eaten the same enchiladas, so the chile should be equally hot. The men continued arguing after the witness suggested they take his dog for a walk. Eventually, Cavazos punched Gutierrez, and the two fought, according to the witness’ account. Cavazos struck Gutierrez enough to leave him bleeding before the fight ended and Cavazos began walking away, according to the affidavit. Gutierrez then allegedly pulled out a handgun and confronted Cavazos, saying, “We’re family! We’re family! How could you do this to me?” the witness told investigators. The witness said Cavazos was about 10 feet away and was not holding a weapon when Gutierrez fired three or four times, striking him in the back. Gutierrez then fled, according to the affidavit. Police said the witness showed investigators a Snapchat message in which Gutierrez allegedly said Cavazos had threatened his life. “Is he really dead?” Gutierrez allegedly wrote. “I did not want to kill him but i didn’t want him to kill me.” Investigators said a handgun belonging to Cavazos was found at least 10 yards from his body.

articles.title: Colorado has logged more than 7,000 bear sightings in 2026, topping its previous full-year record as hungry bears increasingly enter homes, shops and towns across the US West
articles.summary: US News: Matt Errico was sitting on the toilet in his Granby home when he heard strange sounds coming from the corridor. When he went to check, he found two yo.
articles.body: Matt Errico was sitting on the toilet in his Granby home when he heard strange sounds coming from the corridor. When he went to check, he found two young black bears, about the size of golden retrievers, standing in his hallway. After a brief staring match, the bears ran out through the front door. The incident in the small mountain town northwest of Denver is far from unusual. Black bears have also been found inside a Granby vape shop, walked past a school in Santa Fe, New Mexico, and climbed a tree near a farmers market in Denver. Colorado has recorded more than 7,000 bear sightings in 2026, already passing its previous full-year record set in 2019, according to state wildlife figures. A detailed investigation by Reuters explains how severe drought across the American West has pushed hungry bears into towns and cities in record numbers.Record drought cuts wild food suppliesThe rise in bear encounters comes after the driest winter on record. The conditions destroyed much of the natural vegetation, berries, grasses and nuts that make up about 90 per cent of a black bear’s diet. "I've definitely never heard of bears inside, you know, cubs inside someone's house," Errico told Reuters, describing his experience in Granby. Desperate to find enough food before winter, bears are using their strong sense of smell to find food in human settlements. Rubbish, bird feeders and shops can all provide easy sources of food. Wildlife experts are increasingly worried about the long-term effect of environmental changes on bear behaviour. "It is like testing the bears and humans in a new way," Jon Beckmann, a black bear expert, said in comments to Reuters. Climate models predict that the Western United States will continue to become drier. Biologists fear bears could become used to eating human food or change their normal hibernation patterns if warm and dry winters continue.Decades of human expansion into bear territoryThe environmental crisis is happening alongside major population growth across the region. Over the past 50 years, Colorado’s population has more than doubled, pushing housing developments into wildlife corridors and feeding areas around mountain communities such as Vail and Colorado Springs. At the same time, black bear numbers have recovered across much of the West after the animals were almost wiped out in some areas a century ago. State wildlife officials estimate that Colorado is now home to between 17,000 and 20,000 black bears, making them one of the healthiest bear populations among the world’s eight bear species. The combination of more bears, expanding towns and shrinking natural food supplies has increased conflicts between people and wildlife. Colorado has recorded at least six direct bear attacks on people this year.Rising deaths and managing conflictsThe increase in encounters can have deadly results for bears. Hundreds of bears across Western states are being shot, electrocuted or euthanised after entering residential areas. Jonathan Livingston, a spokesperson for Colorado Parks and Wildlife, told Reuters that between 1.5 per cent and 2 per cent of reported sightings end with a bear being euthanised. State authorities generally remove and kill bears that enter occupied homes or show aggressive behaviour towards people. Livingston said early reports from residents give wildlife officers the best chance of scaring bears away with non-lethal methods before the animals learn to depend on human buildings and food. Many encounters begin with simple problems, such as unlocked rubbish bins or bird feeders left outside. But these food sources can bring residents face-to-face with black bears weighing between 200 and 400 pounds and carrying three-to-four-inch claws. Community conservation groups, including the Colorado Bear Coalition, are calling on local authorities to introduce stronger rules requiring bear-resistant rubbish containers. Field biologists warn that the problem could become worse as autumn approaches and bears enter hyperphagia, a period of intense eating when they consume large amounts of food to build fat reserves before winter hibernation. Heather Reich, a Nevada bear expert and former wildlife agency officer, said she is deeply concerned about what could happen in the coming months as bears search more aggressively for food. "We can't imagine how September and October will look. It's going to be Armageddon," Reich told Reuters.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump: ‘I don’t want Canadian anything’
articles.summary: President Trump said Sunday he does not want U.S. businesses to import Canadian goods amid continued tariff tensions between the two countries. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said his tariffs “revived, and indeed saved” the American automobile industry, pointing to profits made by Ford, General Motors and other U.S. car companies during his…
articles.body:
President Trump said Sunday he does not want U.S. businesses to import Canadian goods amid continued tariff tensions between the two countries.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said his tariffs “revived, and indeed saved” the American automobile industry, pointing to profits made by Ford, General Motors and other U.S. car companies during his second term.

The president then called Canada “one of the worst abusers” in trade, after his 50 percent import taxes on $27.6 billion worth of goods imported from Canada went into effect earlier this month.

“They’ve been ripping us off for decades, and it’s going to stop. This should have happened long ago with other Presidents, just as stopping Iran should have happened long ago,” Trump continued, referring to his levies on Canadian goods.

The president also said the Canadian government wants “to be treated like a State, but they aren’t one,” adding, arguing that while he deals “with the Leadership of many Countries,” he finds Canada “to be the worst.”

Trump concluded, “They are entitled no longer!”

The U.S. tariffs apply to numerous Canadian products, including wine, hockey sticks, cement, natural honey and wallpaper.

Overall, the tariffs apply to 5 percent of U.S. imports from Canada. American businesses imported nearly $382 billion worth of goods from the country’s northern neighbor last year, according to U.S. Census Bureau data .

Canada’s retaliatory levies, which are set to go into effect on Sept. 8, will focus on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, the country’s Department of Finance noted earlier this week .

U.S. goods coming from Canada will face tariffs of 15, 25 or 50 percent — with the rate for each product matching the rate imposed by the Trump administration.

articles.title: Packers’ Josh Jacobs placed on commissioner exempt list while he faces misdemeanor charges
articles.summary: Jacobs was arrested in May three days after police were called to his home to investigate a disturbance. He was released from jail the next day.
articles.body: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs has been placed on the NFL’s commissioner exempt list while two misdemeanor charges against him are pending, a move that prevents him from practicing or attending games. Upon request and with the club’s permission, Jacobs may be present at the club’s facility on a reasonable basis for meetings, individual workouts, therapy and rehabilitation and other permitted non-football activities. NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy confirmed Sunday that Jacobs had been placed on the list, a move that comes three days after the charges were filed against him. ESPN first reported the development. The Packers open their season Sept. 13 at Minnesota. Brown County, Wisconsin, District Attorney David Lasee announced Thursday that Jacobs had been charged with battery and criminal damage to property. The charges arose from what police described as a physical confrontation between Jacobs and his girlfriend. Jacobs was arrested on May 26, three days after police were called to his home to investigate a disturbance. He was released from jail the next day. Jacobs’ lawyers — David Z. Chesnoff, Richard A. Schonfeld and Clarence F. Duchac III — issued a statement in response to the NFL’s decision. They noted this move is “an administrative procedure used by the NFL while a matter is being reviewed.” “It is not a final determination,” they said. “Josh respects the NFL process, the Packers, and his Coaches and Teammates. He looks forward to his return to the team and the NFL.” Hobart-Lawrence police officers who responded to the May call said Jacobs’ girlfriend told them she had a lump on her head as a result of Jacobs’ actions. Police said the woman said she had been looking through Jacobs’ phone and saw he was talking to other women and that she threw the phone in anger without breaking it. She told police that Jacobs had her phone and that she told him he could look through it. According to police, the woman indicated she tried to retrieve her phone from Jacobs, but he didn’t return it and instead grabbed her arm and began a struggle that lasted several minutes. They then left the home in separate vehicles before eventually returning. Police said the woman was trying to exit a garage door to get outside when Jacobs grabbed her and threw her to the ground, causing her to hit her head. Police said Jacobs also took the phone from her while she was on the ground. According to the criminal complaint filed last week, surveillance footage from the camera system in the garage corroborated the woman’s statement. Jacobs rushed for 929 yards and 13 touchdowns last season. That followed a 2024 season in which Jacobs ran for 1,329 yards and 15 touchdowns while earning his third Pro Bowl selection. The 28-year-old has rushed for 7,803 yards and 74 touchdowns in his seven-year career, which included five seasons with the Raiders. articles.title: ‘Opening a new chapter’: Syria reopens embassy in Libya after talks
articles.summary: Syrian foreign minister and Libyan PM agree to cooperation committee and reopening of diplomatic missions.
articles.body:
Syria and Libya have agreed to reopen Syria’s embassy in Tripoli, which has been closed for 14 years, and reactivate a committee for coordinating bilateral ties during talks between Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah of Libya’s internationally recognised government and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani.

Al-Shaibani arrived in Tripoli on Sunday to meet with Libyan officials, according to a statement from Libya’s Government of National Unity (GNU).

Libya has been split since 2014 between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, led by Dbeibah, and an eastern administration, led by Osama Hammad and backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar. Representatives of Libya’s rival governments signed a deal on Sunday to hold national elections within two years.

Damascus and Tripoli signed an agreement to reactivate the Libyan-Syrian Joint Higher Committee, a committee at the prime ministerial level tasked with coordinating political, economic and social ties between the two countries.

Dbeibah and al-Shaibani also agreed to open a Syrian consulate in Benghazi, raising the level of diplomatic representation between the two states.

The talks covered security cooperation and counterterrorism, according to the GNU statement. The two sides also discussed consular services and the status of prisoners, detainees and refugees from both countries.

Economically, they addressed unresolved financial dues between Libyan and Syrian institutions. The Syrian foreign minister also met with Libya’s oil and gas minister and the country’s investment authority chief to discuss energy and investment cooperation.

The Syrian embassy in Libya has been closed since 2012 after Libya’s then-Transitional National Council recognised the Syrian opposition and diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed during then-Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s rule.

Syrian opposition forces ousted al-Assad in December 2024, ending 61 years of Baath Party rule.

In August 2025, a Syrian delegation raised the post-Assad Syrian flag over the Tripoli embassy, signalling that its reopening was imminent.

Dbeibah called Sunday’s meeting the start of “a new chapter” in their relations, saying it should be “based on shared interests, practical cooperation and addressing outstanding issues”.

articles.title: Diabetes impacts men, women differently: Study
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: For men, type 2 diabetes more often sets the stage for heart and kidney disease; for women, the greater threat appears to be mental health .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: For men, type 2 diabetes more often sets the stage for heart and kidney disease; for women, the greater threat appears to be mental health problems, a new study tracking nearly 29,000 patients has found.The study, published in PLOS Medicine, followed 28,720 people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2010 and 2020 using linked primary and secondary healthcare records in the UK. Researchers used a multi-state analysis to track the order and timing of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, end-stage renal disease and mental health conditions over a median follow-up of 6.8 years. Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition.Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition, including anxiety, depression or somatoform disorders, after developing diabetes. Such conditions were recorded in 8.1% of women compared with 5.3% of men.Men, meanwhile, were more likely to develop cardiovascular disease or end-stage renal disease, with 8.4% following this trajectory compared with 5.3% of women.Senior endocrinologist Prof Ravinder Goswami of All India Institutes of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) said diabetes can affect men and women differently. Men may develop diabetes at a younger age, while women with diabetes lose the natural protection against heart disease that is usually seen before menopause. The study also found that women with diabetes may have a higher risk of problems related to memory, thinking and mental health.However, he cautioned that these problems may not be caused by diabetes alone, as cognitive and neuropsychiatric problems are generally more common in women. He said doctors should, therefore, watch for these issues while managing diabetes.Hypertension was the most common complication after type-2 diabetes across all age groups and in both sexes. It affected 21.1% of men and 20.2% of women. Men also experienced most complications earlier than women, while women generally had a later onset of events.The study linked diabetes, mental health and mortality, finding that people who developed a mental health condition after diabetes died earlier. Among those with the same disease trajectory, men died on average nine years younger than women.Despite this, women had higher average healthcare utilisation and long-term prescribing than men. The researchers said the lower healthcare use among men in the high-risk mental health trajectory could point to gaps in engagement with healthcare services.The findings point to the need for sex-specific diabetes care, including routine mental health screening, particularly for younger women, and earlier cardiovascular and kidney monitoring for men.The researchers further added that tracking the sequence and timing of complications could help identify patients at higher risk and enable earlier intervention. However, as an observational study, the findings cannot establish cause and effect, and differences in mental health diagnoses may partly reflect healthcare-seeking behaviour.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Urgent search underway for more than 20 people after Grand Canyon flash flood
articles.summary: More than 20 people may be missing after a major flash flood tore through Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch in the Grand Canyon on Aug. 29.
articles.body: More than 20 people may be missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood tore through a remote area of the Grand Canyon, prompting an urgent public plea from the National Park Service.. Grand Canyon National Park said 62 people had been evacuated as of Sunday morning from Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area, where significant flooding hit on Aug. 29. Officials are asking for the public’s help to account for more than 20 people who may have been in the affected area during the flood. "Additional evacuations are planned today," the park said, warning that more thunderstorms and heavy rain are possible Sunday and Monday, raising the threat of further flash flooding, debris flows and rockfall. PARK VISITORS FACE FLOOD DANGER OUT WEST WHILE SEVERE STORMS RIP THROUGH NY, NJ The flooding struck Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area on Aug. 29, according to the National Park Service, adding that nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed. Park staff and the Arizona Department of Public Safety are continuing evacuation and response operations as they work to account for people who may have been caught in the affected corridor. Officials are asking anyone with information about hikers or backpackers who were in the inner canyon along Bright Angel Creek that day to contact investigators. The request also applies to anyone with a campground reservation in the affected area. MULTIPLE HIKERS DEAD AMID SCORCHING GRAND CANYON TEMPERATURES The National Park Service said it is trying to identify people who may have been traveling on the North Kaibab Trail between the North Kaibab Trailhead and Phantom Ranch, staying at Bright Angel Campground or traveling through an area known as "the Box" north of Phantom Ranch. The agency did not release details about the people who may be missing or unaccounted for, including whether they were hikers, campers or park visitors with reservations in the area. articles.title: Dolly Parton’s niece shares emotional tribute after singer’s private funeral
articles.summary: The country star’s funeral Friday was a private affair attended by family members, said her niece Lainey Parton.
articles.body: Dolly Parton was laid to rest in a private funeral service attended by family on Friday, according to her niece. Lainey Parton shared an emotional tribute post on Instagram on Saturday, writing: “This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words.” Parton died Tuesday following a brief battle with cancer at age 80. Her social media pages said that at her request, a small private service would be held for immediate family. Lainey remembered Parton as a loving and inspiring figure who “believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.” “Because she couldn’t have kids of her own, she always made us feel like we were hers. She loved us that way, and I’ll forever be grateful for that,” she wrote. Lainey shared a slew of photos from growing up with Parton, some from childhood and others taken onstage with the country star. Lainey recalled singing with Parton on her 2024 “Smoky Mountain DNA” album, which included various Parton family members. “I was a freshman in high school and SO nervous. But she had a way of making me feel like nothing bad could happen. She made me feel safe, confident, and like I belonged right there beside her,” Lainey recalled. She said the music icon backed her decision to attend beauty school and helped her fund it. “She didn’t just tell me to chase my dreams, she helped me get there,” she said. “I’m so thankful I said yes to the opportunities and memories I got to share with her as my Aunt Dolly, including being in a movie with her. I’m so glad I have those moments to look back on now. I have things I can watch, hear, and hold onto when I miss her,” she continued. While the family — and the world beyond — mourns Parton’s passing, Lainey said she’s holding on to the precious memories she shared with her “granny.” “It still doesn’t feel real that she’s gone. I’m going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there. I’m even going to miss those 4 AM calls, and I’d give anything to see her name pop up on my phone again,” she said. “I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny. Thank you for always believing in me, loving me, and making me feel like I could do anything. I love you, Granny. Always,” she said, concluding her post. The “Jolene” singer hailed from rural Tennessee, born into a large but tight-knit family. She was one of 12 children, and as her own family expanded, Parton maintained an incredibly close relationship with her siblings, nieces and nephews. Her death sparked widespread mourning and emotional tributes from her fans, Hollywood and the music industry. The 11-time Grammy-winning singer-songwriter was more than just an artist. She was an icon who transcended genre and time, a philanthropist focused on children and poverty, and a businesswoman. Parton was preceded in death by her husband of 59 years, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in 2025, and her parents, Avie Lee Caroline Owens and Robert Lee Parton Sr.

articles.title: Right to question not defiance, every dissent not a threat: SC judge
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: In a constitutional democracy like India, govt must listen to citizens, give space for dissent, and have institutions that are accountable .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: In a constitutional democracy like India, govt must listen to citizens, give space for dissent, and have institutions that are accountable to society and do not treat every dissent as a threat, Supreme Court judge Ujjal Bhuyan said on Sunday."In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance. It is an essential expression of citizenship, liberty and constitutional responsibility," Justice Bhuyan said at a convocation ceremony at National Law University, Delhi."If we want a democratic society that respects liberty and difference, that culture has to begin somewhere. It can only begin in our universities. A university... should be one of the first places where the habit of thinking freely begins," he said.A university should be a space where an idea is not accepted merely because it is familiar and where students do not hesitate to ask difficult questions simply because the answer may be uncomfortable,” Justice Bhuyan said.He said India’s Constitution guarantees free speech, thinking and believing differently. “Intolerance begins to undermine that framework when disagreement or dissent is no longer treated as a legitimate difference of opinion but as something that must be silenced, rejected or punished. The ability to live with disagreement is not merely a social virtue. It is the very essence of a liberal constitutional democracy.”Justice Bhuyan said maturity of a democracy is reflected not merely in how it treated opinions that are popular, having the majoritarian mandate, but also in how it responds to opinions that are difficult, unpopular or inconvenient. “The freedom to express an opinion, to disagree with the prevailing view and to participate in public life would be meaningful only when there is space for dissent,” he added.He quoted Justice O Chinnappa Reddy’s 1986 judgment in Bijoe Emmanuel case, in which the judge had said, “Our tradition teaches tolerance; our philosophy preaches tolerance; our constitution practises tolerance; let us not dilute it.”He pointed out that tolerance under our Constitution does not ask us to surrender our individuality. “It recognises that a free society would contain different opinions, beliefs and ways of looking at the world,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Authorities are searching for hikers and campers who may have been trapped in the area.
articles.body: At least 20 people are missing or unaccounted for after flash floods overwhelmed a remote area of the Grand Canyon, including a historic lodge near the bottom of the site, officials said Sunday. The National Park Service is asking for information about anyone who may have been hiking or backpacking along Bright Angel Creek in Arizona, as well as campers with plans to stay at Phantom Ranch or the Bright Angel Campground. Officials are also trying to track down travelers who might have been stranded along the North Kaibab Trail. By Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail. Additional evacuations from Phantom Ranch and the Cottonwood Campground were expected. Park administrators also said that footbridges along Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, “eliminating hiker access across the creek,” and that certain Colorado River crossings were closed while damage is assessed. “The flash flood resulted in significant impacts to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon,” the National Park Service said in a statement. “Grand Canyon National Park staff are continuing to assess damage to trails, bridges, utilities, facilities and other infrastructure.” Phantom Ranch is accessible only by hiking, raft or mule transport. It has been a coveted Grand Canyon destination since it opened in 1922. Colorado River traffic was also shut down because of the risk of floating debris.

articles.title: Hunt intensifies for 900 missing at hydel units, one tunnel head located
articles.summary: South Asia News: NUWAKOT (NEPAL)/DEHRADUN: Time running out for over 900 people missing from Nepal's flood-hit hydropower projects, rescue teams led by Nepalese Army p.
articles.body: NUWAKOT (NEPAL)/DEHRADUN: Time running out for over 900 people missing from Nepal's flood-hit hydropower projects, rescue teams led by Nepalese Army personnel intensified operations to hunt for survivors, particularly at the Upper Trishuli-3A, where they located the tunnel's crown head and began widening an opening to send rescuers inside with oxygen cylinders.While the Independent Power Producers' Association Nepal said 537 workers and staff were unaccounted for across nine projects, Nepal's disaster management authority, NDRRMA, stated that 933 workers from hydropower projects were untraced.The number of dead rose to 810 Sunday - 794 in Nepal and 16 reported in Tibet - with 3,048 missing across both countries, as search ops entered a fifth day. NDRRMA listed 2,502 people missing and Tibet another 546. Nepal said 592 foreign nationals were among those missing, besides 127 Nepalese citizens travelling with foreign groups.MEA said at 5.30pm Sunday that 149 Indian nationals had been rescued in Nepal. Its latest missing-person tally, issued Saturday night, listed 275 Indian nationals missing and another 128 people of Indian origin as uncontactable. India had also not announced a confirmed number of Indian deaths by Sunday evening.Efforts to hunt for survivors at the nine hydropower projects picked up as weather improved slightly. Road access to Upper Trishuli-3A remained cut off, forcing Nepalese Army to airlift excavators, bulldozers and other earth-moving machinery to the project area using helicopters. Joint teams operated the machines through the night despite rain and moved closer to the tunnel entry point.Nepalese Army spokesperson Brig Gen Rajaram Basnet told TOI that the team, which included tunnel experts, had located the crown head - the main section - of Trishuli 3A. "A hole of 2x3ft was dug, which revealed a water surface spanning a diameter of around seven metres and extending to a significant height. An army expert entered the hole and looked for signs of life but with no luck so far," Basnet said."We're now trying to widen the hole area to allow more experts to enter with oxygen cylinders and search for those trapped," he added. By Sunday evening, around 8,500 Army personnel had been deployed across major flood-affected areas for search-and-rescue operations.MEA cautions against relying on changing casualty figuresAt Upper Trishuli-1, around 300 workers were believed to have been trapped inside the tunnel, of whom 254 had been rescued, while search operations continued for the remaining workers. At Upper Trishuli-3B, 91 of the 122 workers earlier reported missing had been rescued and 31 remained unaccounted for, showing how the rescue effort had expanded far beyond the 100-odd workers initially feared trapped at a handful of sites.Nearly 20,000 security personnel had been deployed, while ground and aerial teams continued searches along riverbanks, destroyed settlements and mud-filled tunnels. Nepal foreign secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said, “Our immediate national priority remains clear: to save lives, locate missing persons, rescue them, provide urgent relief to survivors, and ensure that affected Nepalese as well as foreign nationals receive appropriate assistance and support.”As number of the dead and missing kept changing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal cautioned: “We are in a dynamic situation, so figures keep going up and down. Also, we have to reconcile several lists that we are dealing with.”Among the lists of “foreign nationals”, the count of people of Indian origin is likely to be high. Many travellers formally counted as American, British, Australian, Canadian and other nationals were people of Indian origin travelling on foreign passports, several of them on or returning from Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage.In one 77-member group caught in the disaster, 53 were people of Indian origin carrying foreign passports.The Indian picture on the Tibet side was also being counted separately. Chinese authorities said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were among the 546 missing in Gyirong, including 49 Indians, 104 Nepalese, 33 Latvians, 18 Americans, 15 Britons, six Canadians and six Australians.It remained unclear whether the 49 Indians listed in Tibet were already part of MEA’s broader count of 275 missing Indian citizens.Large numbers of Indian pilgrims and travellers stranded on the China side had meanwhile begun moving out. MEA said earlier Sunday that 598 Indians had crossed safely from China into Nepal over two days, while around 900 Indians who remained on the Chinese side were “safe and contactable”. Indian missions in Beijing and Kathmandu remained in touch with Chinese and Nepalese authorities.India intensified its technical assistance. Four relief flights had carried 68.5 tonnes of supplies to Kathmandu, while a 13-member Indian Army tunnel-rescue team with specialist equipment and six forensic teams comprising 19 personnel were sent to assist Nepalese authorities. Sixteen trucks carrying equipment for a 230-foot single-lane modular steel bridge had reached Nepal and equipment for seven more Bailey bridges was being supplied.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1342, Europe suffered its worst flood year in 700 years; scientists now say 16 major floods struck the continent within just three years
articles.summary: Europe News: For centuries, the Magdalena Flood of July 1342 stood out as one of the great flood disasters of medieval Central Europe. A new study published in Nat.
articles.body: For centuries, the Magdalena Flood of July 1342 stood out as one of the great flood disasters of medieval Central Europe. A new study published in Nature suggests the disaster was actually part of something much larger: a run of 16 major floods that hit different parts of Europe between late 1341 and 1343. Researchers led by Andrea Kiss, a historian, medievalist and geographer at TU Wien, pieced the sequence together from more than 1,000 entries in contemporary records and other historical evidence. Four of the floods were classified as extreme events, with estimated return periods of 500 to 1,000 years. The researchers found that 1342 had more great and extraordinary floods than any other year in their 700-year European record, while 1343 ranked among the top 10. The repeated flooding damaged settlements, farmland, roads and other infrastructure, while the disruption contributed to food shortages and wider economic problems. The researchers link the unusual cluster to volcanic activity alongside major changes in the Arctic and North Atlantic climate.How researchers reconstructed 16 medieval floods from historical recordsThe study, Cascading continental-scale floods across Europe in 1342–1343, was published in Nature on August 12, 2026. To reconstruct what happened, the researchers went through more than 1,000 contemporary records describing floods during the period and compared accounts from different parts of Europe. That approach changed the story considerably. Instead of treating the Magdalena Flood as a single exceptional disaster, the researchers found evidence of repeated flooding beginning in eastern and southeastern Europe in November and December 1341. More followed during the winter and spring of 1342, including the Candlemas Flood in February. Then came the Magdalena Flood in July, followed by further major floods affecting northern Italy, the Mediterranean region and the Carpathian Basin later that year. The pattern continued into 1343. Taken together, the records show that Europe was dealing with one major flood after another across several seasons, rather than experiencing one unusually destructive summer.Why the repeated floods caused such widespread destructionThe timing made the damage particularly difficult to deal with. Communities that had barely begun repairing roads, bridges and buildings could be hit again by another flood months, or sometimes weeks, later. The Magdalena Flood caused extensive destruction in parts of southern Germany, while other events affected major river systems including the Rhine and Danube. Settlements were damaged, farmland was inundated and transport routes were disrupted. Mills and river crossings were especially important pieces of infrastructure because losing them could interfere with both food production and movement between communities. The effects did not end when the water receded. Damaged farmland meant lower agricultural production, while interruptions to transport made it harder to move food and other supplies. The study describes the wider period as having major socioeconomic consequences, with flooding, hunger and disease contributing to substantial loss of life.What volcanic eruptions and Arctic changes may have had to do with the floodsThe sheer number of major floods raised another question: why did so many occur within such a short period? The researchers looked at climate conditions around the same time and found a possible explanation involving both volcanic activity and changes in the Arctic and North Atlantic. Several eruptions occurred around the beginning of the period, while climate evidence points to significant changes in Arctic sea ice. The idea is not that one volcano directly caused all 16 floods. Instead, the authors propose that a combination of volcanic eruptions and multi-year changes in Arctic sea ice altered atmospheric circulation across the Northern Hemisphere. Those changes may have created conditions that made intense rainfall and flooding more likely in parts of Europe. It is a reminder that extreme weather does not always happen in isolation. Large-scale changes in the climate system can create a period in which several otherwise unusual events occur close together.Why the Magdalena Flood became famous while the wider sequence was forgottenThe Magdalena Flood has survived in European historical memory far more prominently than many of the other floods identified in the study. That may partly be a consequence of how disasters are recorded and remembered. A flood that leaves behind particularly detailed written accounts, physical markers or a strong local memory can remain visible for centuries. Another disaster, even one that was highly destructive, can gradually disappear from the historical record. Looking at records from across Europe changes that perspective. What appears to be one exceptional flood when viewed from a single region becomes part of a much broader pattern when accounts from different river basins are compared. The researchers also identify the 1342–1343 sequence as an important period in the development of European flood protection. Repeated disasters forced communities to think more seriously about how to prepare for severe flooding rather than treating every event as an isolated catastrophe.What Europe's medieval flood sequence means for modern flood riskThe floods of 1342 and 1343 offer a useful warning for modern Europe because they show how quickly extreme events can pile up. Flood planning often focuses on the likelihood and expected severity of individual events. But a community hit by several major floods in succession faces a different problem. Repairs may not be finished, emergency resources may be depleted and damaged infrastructure can make the next disaster even harder to manage. The medieval record shows that unusually severe floods can cluster across relatively short periods and affect different regions in succession. More than six centuries later, the sequence of 1341–1343 offers a broader lesson: Europe's worst flood periods are not necessarily defined by one extraordinary river overflowing its banks. Sometimes the real danger is what happens when one major disaster is followed by another, and then another, before the continent has had time to recover.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: CJP netas not saints... nothing wrong in having political ambitions: Wangchuk
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has said Abhijit Dipke and his fellow organisers of the Cockroach Janta Party movement appear to have polit.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has said Abhijit Dipke and his fellow organisers of the Cockroach Janta Party movement appear to have political ambitions, but there is nothing objectionable in this as long as the student platform retains its non-party character.Wangchuk, in a Prakhar Gupta Xperience podcast, said Dipke and the others had not disclosed any plans to him and his view was based on his own assessment. “Political ambition is very normal,” he said. “Past political connections I don’t care about, present and future political aspirations are not a problem.”“They are not such saints that they want absolutely nothing and are doing all this entirely selflessly,” he said, referring to the possibility that the organisers had personal or political aspirations.Assessing their suitability for leadership, Wangchuk described the organisers as “well meaning”, “quite skilled” and “above average”.“Well meaning but unskilled” could create difficulties, while “very skilled but ill meaning” would pose a much greater danger, he said.Asked whether they could become corrupt, Wangchuk said he had seen no such indications. “People go through changes, and I hope they won’t,” he said.Wangchuk said the organisers could join an existing party or launch a new one later, but must not turn the CJP platform into their political vehicle. He said he had advised them to preserve it as a “neutral, apolitical pressure group”, arguing that this would help retain the trust of supporters who saw it as a students’ movement rather than an organisation aligned with BJP, Congress or AAP.Wangchuk acknowledged that his own standards sometimes led him to expect public figures to have no political ambition. That, he said, could be unrealistic because the organisers were ordinary people entitled to pursue political careers. Beginning such a career by championing an education-related cause could, in fact, be positive.He also expressed hope that participation in the movement would help them emerge as more mature and grounded politicians. “I am actually happy about that,” Wangchuk said of their taking up public issues.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body: Rapper and streamer Darryl Dwayne “DDG” Granberry Jr. has sparked a debate over who GTA 6 is really made for. During a recent livestream, DDG argued that younger players cannot fully understand the excitement around Rockstar Games’ next Grand Theft Auto title because they did not grow up playing its older games. He pointed to the long wait between GTA 5 and GTA 6 and said longtime fans had experienced the series when its graphics were much less advanced. His comments later led him to claim that he was receiving death threats from young Instagram users.DDG says younger GTA 6 fans missed the old gamesDDG brought up his own experience with the series while discussing the excitement around GTA 6. He noted that GTA 5 arrived when he was 15 and said he is now 30.The rapper then argued that younger fans did not have the same experience with the franchise as older players who had followed it for years.DDG said:“GTA 5 came out when I was 15. N**** I'm 30 now. This game ain't for you young n****. That's what I'm trying to get through y'all fking brain. All you young a n**** that keep saying, 'GTA 6, GTA 6,' this is for the old n****. We waited for this sht, n***. We waited 15 years.”He continued by pointing to older games such as GTA: Vice City and argued that younger players never had to experience the less advanced graphics of earlier titles.The comments drew attention online, and DDG later claimed that some young users had taken their reaction too far. In a post on X, he wrote that he was receiving “death threats from 10-year-olds” on Instagram.Rockstar Games shows more of GTA 6 ahead of November releaseDDG’s comments came just as Rockstar Games gave fans a much longer look at GTA 6. The studio released Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look on August 27, first on Netflix and later on YouTube. Rockstar said the footage was captured entirely from the PlayStation 5.The extended look focuses on the game’s two main characters, Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos. Their story follows the pair as they become caught in a criminal conspiracy across Leonida, the fictional state that includes Vice City. Rockstar describes their relationship as central to the game as they are forced to depend on each other after a planned job goes wrong.The footage also gives players a closer look at Leonida’s different locations, along with shoot-outs, driving sequences and character switching. articles.title: Fears of more flooding in Nepal, and NASA launches next-generation telescope: Weekend Rundown
articles.summary: Authorities in Nepal have warned of further flooding after heavy rainfall, as China sheds more light on the scale of the disaster in its Tibet region.
articles.body: Authorities in Nepal have warned of further flooding after heavy rainfall, as China sheds more light on the scale of the disaster in its Tibet region. Five days after floodwaters unleashed by a glacier collapse buried communities under thick mud, rescuers in Nepal were still struggling to reach devastated areas as the full extent of the destruction came into focus. “The disaster here is overwhelming,” Ferrin Cole, an operations director with the U.S.-based Crisis Response International, told NBC News on Sunday. “The flood that came down that mountain just wiped out cities. We’re going in as fast as we can to get people the help that they need.” About 100 Americans are among those missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region, the State Department said Saturday. In Nepal, the death toll has risen to 781, with more than 2,500 people still missing, including 592 foreign nationals, according to the country’s disaster agency. The Nepal Tourism Board said 289 foreign nationals have been rescued. China has separately reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing in the Tibet region, including 261 foreign nationals. It remains unclear how much overlap exists between the Chinese and Nepali missing-person counts. NASA launches its next-generation space telescope NASA on Sunday launched a next-generation space telescope expected to survey hundreds of millions of stars and billions of galaxies, while helping unlock clues to dark energy, dark matter and some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off at 7:26 a.m. ET from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida atop a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. After 31 minutes and 41 seconds, the telescope separated from the rocket and began its journey to orbit around the second sun-Earth Lagrange point, a gravitational balance point roughly 1 million miles from Earth. Often compared to the iconic Hubble Space Telescope, the Roman observatory is expected to revolutionize humanity’s understanding of the universe — and our place in it. U.S. forces strike Iranian rocket launchers on Strait of Hormuz in first military action in weeks U.S. forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in their first military action in a month Sunday. Iran swiftly vowed to retaliate for what it called a deadly attack. Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command. The U.S. military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes. The attack comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure — rather than military action — to try to end its war with Iran. ‘Meet the Press’ Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, renewed his call for free and fair elections in Venezuela, just two days after the Trump administration announced that the U.S. would take over 65 billion barrels of oil from the South American nation. “There need to be democratic, free elections in Venezuela,” Cruz told NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” adding later in the interview that elections should take place there “midway through next year.” The senator also praised the oil deal, adding that he doesn’t think the U.S. needs to prioritize free and fair elections in Venezuela over the deal. Rep. Jiames Clyburn, D-S.C., told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats should not prioritize impeaching Trump if they win control of the House in the upcoming midterm elections, but instead should focus on making life more affordable for Americans. The South Carolina representative also said that he regretted his support for Clarence Thomas during the Supreme Court justice’s confirmation hearings in 1991. “I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences,” Clyburn said. Politics in brief Nominee’s apology: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, apologized for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March, which he tied to Israel’s actions in the Middle East.The lake divide: Google Maps has changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for U.S. users to reflect Trump’s executive order renaming the lake, according to ​a Google statement. Minnesota Supreme Court rejects Mike Lindell’s bid to recount primary loss The Minnesota Supreme Court on Saturday rejected Mike Lindell’s bid for a full recount of his loss in the state’s GOP gubernatorial primary. Chief Justice Natalie E. Hudson wrote in a six-page ruling that the Minnesota Secretary of State’s Office and its State Canvassing Board provided a recount plan that follows the law and are “not committing any wrongful act, omission, or error” as Lindell claimed. The MyPillow founder, a longtime 2020 election denier, told NBC News in a phone call that he plans to appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court. “I’m willing to pay even more money. I don’t care what it costs,” Lindell said. He previously pledged to pay an estimated $825,000 to cover a full hand recount and audit of the race but refused to pay the money on Monday, which marked the state’s deadline. Taylor Swift donates $50,000 to mom injured while saving teens from highway crash Taylor Swift donated $50,000 to help a Rhode Island mother who was left seriously injured in a car accident last month, NBC News confirmed. Ashley Taunton was driving on I-95 in Hopkinton during a torrential rainstorm when she saw a car in front of her hydroplane off the road. She pulled over and ran to help the teenagers inside the crashed vehicle, her husband told NBC affiliate WJAR of Providence. As she was helping them, another vehicle hydroplaned and barreled toward them, he said, leaving her with severe injuries. After Swift’s donation, Taunton posted on social media: “This is unbelievable and I am overwhelmed with gratitude.” In case you missed it Iran’s Supreme Leader ​Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim countries, particularly those in the Gulf, to unite against what he called their “real enemy,” in a written statement.A Russian strike on a Ukrainian warehouse killed 38 people in the war’s deadliest attack this year. Four people are still missing, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on social media. Masked Israeli settlers attacked and injured a Palestinian woman and members of an NBC News team reporting in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Saturday.At least eight people died after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off northern Cyprus on Sunday, Turkish media reported. A search is underway for those still missing.Milo Yiannopoulos, a controversy-baiting internet personality who once vehemently backed Trump, was deported to the United Kingdom, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said. Four baby goats from a North Carolina mobile petting zoo tested positive for rabies and were euthanized.Icelanders voted to reject a reopening of European Union membership talks. The government had framed it as a matter of national security, but voters were instead focused on interest rates, fishing rights and the cost of living.

articles.title: DHS denies reports of torture, beatings and medical neglect in ICE detention
articles.summary: The Homeland Security Department (DHS) on Sunday denied a report in The New York Times about harsh treatment of migrants in immigration detention facilities. “Another day and another hoax about ICE detention from the @nytimes,” DHS wrote on social platform X. “The media is clearly desperate for these false allegations to be true.” The Times…
articles.body:
The Homeland Security Department (DHS) on Sunday denied a report in The New York Times about harsh treatment of migrants in immigration detention facilities.

“Another day and another hoax about ICE detention from the @nytimes,” DHS wrote on social platform X . “The media is clearly desperate for these false allegations to be true.”

The Times reported Sunday on 10 deportees who said they experienced or witnessed what they described as abusive or violent treatment by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.

The Trump administration later deported the migrants to third countries such as Liberia, despite them not having any ties to the African country. The administration has reportedly struck deportation deals with at least 35 countries.

Leonardo Sánchez, a Cuban migrant, told the Times that ICE officers forced him and three other deportees onto the tarmac in the Liberian capital of Monrovia, after they refused to disembark.

The federal agents then twisted the migrants’ handcuffs, pinned them to the ground and pressed their knees directly onto the their necks, Sánchez recalled.

“They didn’t treat us like people, like human beings,” Carlos Téllez-Sanchez, a Venezuelan whom the administration deported to Liberia, told the paper. “They can say or do anything to you and there’s nothing you can do.”

Other deportees said ICE officials denied medical care to migrants, including pregnant women, and housed detainees in detention centers where up to 50 people shared one toilet.

But the DHS denied those claims, saying, “NO ONE is being tortured, denied medical care, or beaten in ICE detention facilities.”

The department also argued the report in the Times, which it called “GARBAGE,” is one of many “fueling” an increase in “assaults” against ICE officers.

DHS officials said in January that death threats against its law enforcement officers were up 8,000 percent, with assaults up by more than 1,300 percent.

articles.title: Mamdani turns on New York City teachers union with lawsuit blocking pay raises for educators
articles.summary: The United Federation of Teachers filed a motion to intervene after New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sued to block paraprofessional bonuses he once backed.
articles.body: The United Federation of Teachers (UFT), New York City's largest teachers union, is fighting back against Mayor Zohran Mamdani's efforts to block a city-backed pay raise for education paraprofessionals, after the group previously endorsed him last year. Last month, the New York City Council unanimously passed the "RESPECT Check Act," which would offer up to a $10,000-bonus for education paraprofessionals. Though Mamdani supported a version of the bill in the past, he has since spoken out against it, arguing that it violates New York state's Taylor Law, which protects public employees' rights to negotiate issues like compensation. His administration later filed a lawsuit to stop the law from being enacted Aug. 19. FLASHBACK: MAMDANI'S HISTORY OF DODGING QUESTIONS ABOUT WHERE HE STANDS ON KEY ISSUES In response, the UFT filed a motion to intervene last week, preparing to take the issue to court if Mamdani continues to fight the measure. "We knew this lawsuit was a possibility, and we were prepared," UFT President Michael Mulgrew told Fox News Digital in a statement. "The RESPECT check law, which was unanimously passed by City Council on July 16, was carefully drafted to make sure that it did not violate the state’s Taylor Law, which governs collective bargaining." He added, "The City Council would not have introduced — let alone passed — this bill if it were illegal, and we would not have supported a bill that threatened our collective bargaining rights. This moment is an opportunity for Mayor Mamdani to create a new, fairer system and build the kind of city he said he wanted to lead. This administration must keep its promises, and we won’t stop until it does." MAMDANI'S PLAN TO CUT GIFTED PROGRAMS IN NYC SCHOOLS DRIVING PARENTS TO COMPETITIVE PRIVATE EDUCATION: REPORT Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment but did not immediately receive a reply. In a statement to Fox News Digital, the city council pointed to a joint statement made by City Council Speaker Julie Menin and council member Carmen De La Rosa on Mamdani's lawsuit earlier this month. "Every member of the Council, in a unanimous and bipartisan vote, supported the RESPECT Check Act because it is unacceptable that paraprofessionals who support some of our highest-need students are earning as little as $32,000 a year. This law is not only the right thing to do, it is also the fiscally responsible thing to do, helping address the staffing shortages that contribute to the City’s $1.5 billion in Carter case costs. The Council will vigorously defend the law," the statement read. NEW YORK CITY'S DECLINING PUBLIC SCHOOL ENROLLMENT PROJECTED TO LOSE OVER 150K MORE AS POPULATION DECLINES The UFT previously endorsed Mamdani after he secured the Democratic nomination for New York City mayor in July 2025. Despite the lawsuit, Mamdani said in a news conference last week that discussions with Menin and the UFT have been "productive," adding that he does not oppose a pay raise for paraprofessionals.
